clue.text: Slowly executed movement gets a soldier into trouble

indicators.note: gets ... into tells us the first pieces are placed inside the word for trouble

parts.note: ado is fuss or trouble, as in much ado
GI is an American private soldier

explanation.surface: A piece of music played slowly lands a soldier in hot water.
explanation.definitionFit: An adagio is a musical passage or movement marked to be played at a slow tempo.

clue.text: People's leader — such as Lincoln?

explanation.surface: A national leader, perhaps an American president like Lincoln.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is the biblical patriarch who led the Hebrew people; the second is Lincoln's first name, the question mark flagging the example.
explanation.definitionFit: The patriarch of Genesis is father of the Israelites, and President Lincoln's forename was the same.

clue.text: Bill is not keen about raising it

indicators.note: about means going round, so the word for not keen surrounds the other piece

parts.note: adverse means hostile or opposed, so not keen

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising means the word it is read upwards, so backwards

explanation.surface: Someone is reluctant to bring up the matter of a bill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'raising' reverses the small word inside the container. 'Bill' is a verb here: to bill a show is to publicise it.
explanation.definitionFit: To bill an event is to promote it in posters and announcements.

clue.text: Reformed ladies highly thought of

indicators.note: reformed means made over into a new shape, so the letters of ladies are rearranged

explanation.surface: Women who have mended their ways are now held in high regard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reformed' asks for the letters of LADIES to be rearranged. The definition reads as a noun: things held in high esteem.
explanation.definitionFit: Principles or standards one most esteems and aims at are one's cherished goals.

clue.text: Criticism comes from loyal chap to striker

parts.note: a brick is old British slang for a reliable, good-hearted fellow
a bat is something that hits a ball

explanation.surface: Hard words come from a faithful friend aimed at a batsman.
explanation.walkthrough: Calling someone 'a brick' is dated British praise for a dependable friend.
explanation.definitionFit: A brickbat is literally a missile thrown in anger, hence a harsh remark or rebuke.

clue.text: Depend on entirely? Not half!

indicators.note: not half means dropping the first half of the word entirely, keeping its back four letters

explanation.surface: A speaker asks whether to trust something completely and gets an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it tells you to throw away half of 'entirely'.
explanation.definitionFit: To count on or trust someone is to place one's dependence upon them.

clue.text: Enclosure is not at all simple

explanation.surface: A fenced area that proves anything but straightforward.
explanation.walkthrough: One sense is a walled-in area, as with a prison or animal pen; the other is the adjective for something made of several parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A walled area for buildings or animals, and also an adjective for something made up of several elements rather than one.

clue.text: Settle in or out of court

explanation.surface: Reaching agreement, whether before a judge or privately.
explanation.walkthrough: A settle is a long wooden seat with a high back. Judges sit on the bench in court, and a park seat is one out of court; the legal sense of settle is misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: A settle is a long seat; magistrates sit on one in court, and garden seats stand outside.

clue.text: Late but not unwilling

parts.note: late here means deceased, and not unwilling is read as not without a will, describing someone who died having made one

explanation.surface: Someone arrives behind time but is happy enough to come.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'unwilling' as 'un-will-ing', lacking a will.
explanation.definitionFit: The legal term for a dead person who left a valid will behind.

clue.text: Give notice

parts.note: notice here is a critic's write-up of a play or book, so giving one is writing an assessment

explanation.surface: Telling an employer you are leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Give notice' suggests resigning, but a notice is also a critic's piece in the paper.
explanation.definitionFit: A critic's published appraisal of a show is called a notice, and writing one is the verb sense.

clue.text: Employees in steelworks making components

indicators.note: in places the staff inside the rearranged metal
works is read as a verb, the letters of steel being worked into a new order

parts.note: the men are the workforce

explanation.surface: Workers in a steel mill produce parts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'steelworks' must be split in two: its first half is the fodder and 'works' is the anagram signal, giving ELETS around the workers.
explanation.definitionFit: The basic parts or constituents of something are its building blocks.

clue.text: Soldiers take in our weapons

indicators.note: take in means the soldiers' word holds the next word inside it

parts.note: an army is a body of soldiers

explanation.surface: Troops collect our arms.
explanation.definitionFit: An armoury is a store of arms, so it stands for the weaponry held there.

clue.text: Colourful display of arms

parts.note: arms here are coats of arms, the bright shields and devices of noble families, not weapons or limbs

explanation.surface: A vivid show of weaponry, as at a military parade.
explanation.definitionFit: The art of designing and recording coats of arms, full of bright tinctures.

clue.text: She may go out for pantihose, but not net

indicators.note: go out suggests the letters are thrown into disorder once some are removed

explanation.surface: A woman might wear tights rather than fishnet stockings for an evening out.
explanation.walkthrough: Take NET out of PANTIHOSE, leaving P,A,I,H,O,S, and rearrange those; 'but not net' names the letters taken away.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, here standing for any woman.

clue.text: Base and vicious, determined to torment

parts.note: a bed is a base or foundation, as in a road bed
evil means wicked, cruel or vicious

explanation.surface: A low and spiteful person sets out to plague someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Base' looks like an adjective meaning low, but it is the noun: a bed.
explanation.definitionFit: To plague or harass someone persistently, as if by a demon.

clue.text: Letters man read out

indicators.note: read out means spoken aloud, so we want a word sounding like the one for man

parts.note: a man is a male

explanation.surface: A man reads correspondence aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Post delivered to you is the letters and parcels that arrive.

clue.text: How italian and German cipher directions become insecure

parts.note: come is Italian for how
und is German for and
a cipher is a zero, the figure 0
N and E, north and east, are compass directions

explanation.surface: A spy asks how Italian and German codes lose their security.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that comes loose or falls apart, like a knot or a plan, stops being secure.

clue.text: Smile upon frolic that's spontaneous

indicators.note: frolic suggests playful capering, so the letters of smile upon jump about into a new order

explanation.surface: A grin breaks out at a bit of playful fun.
explanation.definitionFit: Acting suddenly without forethought is doing something unplanned.

clue.text: A female in Minnesota is likely to be

definitions.text: A female in Minnesota is likely to be

indicators.note: in places the girl's name inside the state abbreviation

parts.note: MN is the postal abbreviation for Minnesota
Erica is a female name

explanation.surface: A woman living in Minnesota will probably have a certain nationality.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the recipe and the definition: anyone in Minnesota is likely to be a US citizen.
explanation.definitionFit: Minnesota is a US state, so its residents are mostly citizens of the United States.

clue.text: Trading centre quick to accept a discarded currency

indicators.note: to accept means the word for quick takes the other pieces inside it

parts.note: fleet means swift or quick
the mark was the German currency replaced by the euro

explanation.surface: A busy market quickly takes on a defunct coin.
explanation.walkthrough: The Deutschmark was abandoned when Germany adopted the euro.
explanation.definitionFit: An open-air market selling second-hand goods is a place of buying and selling.

clue.text: Free beers if this is thrown

definitions.text: Free beers if this is thrown

indicators.note: free means let loose, so the letters of beers if are released into a new order

explanation.surface: A bar promises free drinks if a plastic disc is thrown.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both definition and wordplay: 'Free' rearranges BEERS IF, and the toy is the thing thrown.
explanation.definitionFit: A plastic flying disc tossed between players in parks and on beaches.

clue.text: Lean over table

explanation.surface: Tilt across a piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: A ship that heels over is said to list; a list is also a tabulated record.
explanation.definitionFit: A tilting ship leans to one side; and a catalogue or schedule of items is a tabulation.

clue.text: Setting out, steer ship inside locks

indicators.note: inside places the vessel abbreviation within the rearranged letters
setting out means laying the letters of steer out afresh in a new order

parts.note: SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: Departing, someone navigates a vessel into canal locks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setting out' rearranges the steering word to TREES. 'locks' means hair, not canal gates.
explanation.definitionFit: Long locks of hair are flowing tresses.

clue.text: Bill joins a spy organisation as a plant

parts.note: AC is short for account, a bill
the CIA is the US intelligence agency

explanation.surface: Someone named Bill joins the CIA as an undercover agent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a spy planted undercover, but it is a tree or shrub.
explanation.definitionFit: The wattle or thorn tree genus is a flowering shrub or tree.

clue.text: Where teachers teach or instruct

explanation.surface: Teachers in class or giving instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: A form is a British school class, so teachers teach 'in form'.
explanation.definitionFit: A school class is a form, so teaching happens inside one; and to tell or educate someone is to apprise them.

clue.text: A number of fingers

parts.note: number is read as numb-er, something that makes fingers numb with cold

explanation.surface: Counting how many digits there are.
explanation.walkthrough: 'number' is not a count but 'numb-er': what numbs fingers.
explanation.definitionFit: Freezing weather leaves the fingers cold and numb.

clue.text: Discipline lacking in follower

indicators.note: lacking means the following word is missing from the first word

explanation.surface: A follower without self-control.
explanation.definitionFit: An adherent of a teacher, such as one of the apostles.

clue.text: Save up to get a brass instrument

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for save is read upwards, so backwards

parts.note: but means except or save, as in all but one

explanation.surface: Putting money aside to buy a brass instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Save' is not putting money by but the preposition 'except'.
explanation.definitionFit: A large low-pitched valved brass wind.

clue.text: Organisation sending the work to you at home

definitions.text: Organisation sending the work to you at home

parts.words: Organisation sending the work to you at home
parts.note: the work is a literary work, a volume posted to members' homes rather than a job or task

explanation.surface: An agency that sets you up working from home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the work' suggests employment, but it is a book sent by post to subscribers.
explanation.definitionFit: A subscription society that posts chosen volumes to members' homes.

clue.text: Balances notes in the music lesson

explanation.surface: Weighing up notes taken during a music class.
explanation.walkthrough: Balances are weighing devices; musical pupils practise runs of notes up and down.
explanation.definitionFit: Weighing machines, and the graded runs of notes music pupils practise.

clue.text: European schoolboy embraces school head

indicators.note: embraces means the schoolboy's word holds the next piece inside it

parts.note: an Etonian is a pupil at Eton College, the English public school

indicators.note: head means the first letter of the word school

explanation.surface: A European pupil hugs the headmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: ETONIAN is a pupil of Eton College, a famous English boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from Estonia, a Baltic country, is a native of that part of Europe.

clue.text: Worries with second stroke

parts.note: cares are worries

explanation.surface: Anxieties come with a second blow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stroke' is a gentle touch, not a blow or a seizure.
explanation.definitionFit: To touch or pet gently and affectionately.
